target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, workplace safety, and quality of life
objection: AG2 argues that AG1 assumes AI’s benefits automatically outweigh its harms. He says AI is not good for society overall because it predictably creates economic harm, weakens critical thinking, reproduces racism, and threatens privacy.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is overall harmful because its deployment predictably harms workers, learners, equity, and privacy
objection: AG1 objects that AG2 is assuming a worst-case deployment trajectory. He argues the harms are not unavoidable and can be reduced through design, oversight, and policy, while AI’s benefits are real.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can reliably manage AI risks through protections, audits, fairness testing, and privacy controls
objection: AG2 says this assumes governance can reliably outpace harm, which is not warranted. He argues accountability is structurally weak because many models are proprietary black boxes, human oversight can become rubber-stamping, power asymmetries block meaningful control, and mitigation only reduces harms locally while scaling applications expands errors and discrimination.

target: AG2’s claim that weak accountability and incentives mean AI cannot be good for society
objection: AG1 responds that hard regulation does not mean something is not good. He says policy can reduce risk rather than eliminate it, the counterfactual matters because rejecting AI preserves current problems, and targeted rules can allow high-value uses while restricting high-stakes automated decisions.

target: AG1’s argument that AI can still be net good if governance reduces risks and society can choose beneficial uses
objection: AG2 argues AI introduces qualitatively different harms—especially faster manipulation and surveillance—that governance cannot contain. He says AI accelerates misinformation and deepfakes, enables the same infrastructure to be repurposed for discriminatory or surveillance uses, and creates irreversible harms such as privacy violations and reputational or democratic damage.

target: AG2’s claim that AI broadly worsens society by enabling manipulation and surveillance faster than oversight can contain
objection: AG1 objects that AG2 is focusing only on offensive misuse and ignoring AI’s defensive uses. He says AI can help detect deepfakes and misinformation, privacy and reputational harms already exist today, and AI can be deployed selectively in safer, high-benefit domains.

target: AG1’s claim that defensive AI and verification tools offset AI’s harmful uses
objection: AG2 says dual-use capability does not neutralize harm; it entrenches the same system. He argues the detection-versus-deception dynamic becomes a cat-and-mouse arms race, defenses still depend on data and infrastructure that expand surveillance, and many harms happen before they can be remediated.

target: AG2’s claim that defensive AI and arms-race dynamics prove AI is net harmful
objection: AG1 objects that an arms race is not proof of net harm, just a reason to invest in safeguards. He also says privacy-preserving defensive systems can avoid mass surveillance, and staged rollout with strict rules can contain misuse while preserving benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards, staged rollout, and privacy-preserving techniques can manage AI risks
objection: AG2 argues this repeatedly fails in real markets because profit incentives and regulatory capture push companies toward minimum viable compliance. He says companies favor fast, cheap deployment; provenance systems still create incentives to collect and retain information; and fragmented procurement and subcontracting make continuous monitoring too difficult.

target: AG2’s claim that market incentives make responsible AI unrealistic
objection: AG1 counters that many transformative technologies are governed imperfectly but still yield net benefits under rules, liability, and audits. He argues stronger enforceable accountability can improve outcomes, and that partial safeguards already deliver health, accessibility, and safety benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that liability, audits, and procurement rules can make AI safe enough for net social benefit
objection: AG2 says AI harms are systemic, hard to attribute, and scale faster than audits or liability can keep up. Because causality is murky, models change continuously, and opacity blocks contestability, he says accountability mechanisms fail in practice and harmful outcomes keep scaling.

target: AG2’s claim that accountability fails because AI is opaque, changing, and hard to attribute
objection: AG1 replies that accountability can be continuous and layered rather than one-time. He says logging and version control can improve attribution, audits can be ongoing, and procedural safeguards like notice, reasons, appeals, and human review can create real recourse.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous logging, versioning, and procedural recourse solve accountability problems
objection: AG2 argues the proposed fixes intensify privacy surveillance and still will not scale. He says traceability requires collecting sensitive data, meaningful contestability for millions of interactions is impractical, and institutions become dependent on AI systems, making harmful rollbacks difficult.

target: AG2’s claim that traceability and recourse inevitably worsen privacy and are unscalable
objection: AG1 says accountability can be privacy-preserving and risk-tiered. He proposes data minimization, retention limits, encryption, aggregated metrics, differential privacy, and targeted recourse only for high-stakes uses, with pause/rollback triggers and version pinning to handle dependency.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving, risk-tiered accountability can fix AI harms
objection: AG2 says such designs are unreliable in practice and do not address persistent social harms. He argues even minimal logging normalizes surveillance infrastructure, companies will weaken safeguards under cost pressure, bias spreads beyond high-stakes uses, and cognitive offloading harms are irreversible because they occur during use.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy-preserving accountability, risk-tiering, and safeguards are still insufficient
objection: AG1 says AI can be governed as assistive infrastructure rather than autonomous decision-making, reducing bias spread and irreversibility. He argues decision support is better than automated judgment, guardrails can be mandated through procurement, bias can be audited at intermediate stages, and tutoring can be designed as scaffolding instead of outsourcing.

target: AG1’s claim that assistive AI, human-in-the-loop use, and scaffolding reduce the core harms
objection: AG2 argues that even assistive AI still shapes behavior at scale and inherits the same structural risks. He says recommendations steer outcomes even when humans have final say, automation bias undermines learning, and procurement guardrails cannot eliminate persuasive interfaces and behavioral gatekeeping.

target: AG2’s claim that any behavioral influence from assistive AI makes it harmful overall
objection: AG1 objects that not all influence is harmful and that safeguards can preserve user agency. He argues AI recommendations can be optional and clearly labeled, explanations and uncertainty can reduce blind following, and AI can also reduce bias and improve access for marginalized groups.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-in, explanations, and accessibility benefits make assistive AI net positive
objection: AG2 says opt-in is often illusory in institutions, explanations can mislead users, accessibility tools do not offset broader harms, and the same AI infrastructure can still support discrimination, surveillance, and privacy loss.

target: AG2’s claim that institutional use makes opt-in illusory and that accessibility benefits do not matter
objection: AG1 says the issue is risk-tiered deployment, not rejection of AI. He argues real alternatives can be mandated, explanations can be standardized and audited, and accessibility tools can be built with privacy-reducing designs while still delivering important benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-tiered licensing can safely distinguish low-risk assistive uses from high-risk automated decisions
objection: AG2 argues risk-tiering is too brittle because AI systems are general-purpose and use cases drift. He says low-risk tools become gating tools, models can be repurposed across contexts, alternatives are often removed in practice, and auditing becomes either underenforced or too costly.

target: AG2’s claim that risk-tiered licensing is too brittle to work
objection: AG1 says drift and repurposing can be prevented with capability limits, workflow restrictions, procurement rules, and automated certification. He argues the problem is governance design, not AI itself, and that society can keep the benefits while constraining high-risk uses.

target: AG1’s claim that capability limits, procurement, and certification can reliably prevent drift and repurposing
objection: AG2 argues enforcement gaps are structural because every integration point, update, and vendor relationship would need monitoring. He says even approved assistive uses create spillover, economic harms occur in low-risk support roles too, and bias and privacy problems spread through the ecosystem rather than staying contained.

target: AG2’s claim that spillover and enforcement gaps make AI categorically not good
objection: AG1 says spillover means governance must be impact-based and conditionally scalable, not that AI is inherently bad. He argues layered constraints can still improve average outcomes, measurable benchmarks can govern scaling, labor harms are policy-fixable, and supply-chain-wide standards can reduce bias and privacy risks.
